subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
passage:
Hemant: Omkar, I am at the hardware shop and the owner only speaks Bengali. I need a hinge for the cupboard
Omkar: Show him the broken one
Hemant: I did. Then I drew a little door with my finger, opening and closing 😅
Omkar: And?
Hemant: He gave me a lock. Wrong thing
Omkar: Take a photo of the hinge and show it, then say "this one" and point
Hemant: Good idea. Also he nodded in a way I could not read. Yes or no?
Omkar: Ask again with the photo
Hemant: Done. He is smiling and opening a drawer. Fingers crossed 🤞

qa.q: What did Hemant need from the hardware shop?
qa.a: He needed a hinge for the cupboard.

qa.q: Why was Hemant unsure about the owner's nod, and what did he feel?
qa.a: He could not read whether the nod meant yes or no, and he was uneasy after being handed the wrong item. The nod might have been polite or confirming, so he wanted to check.

qa.q: What did Omkar suggest to avoid another mistake?
qa.a: He suggested showing a photo of the hinge and saying "this one" while pointing, so the request is confirmed with an image.

qa.q: How might the shop owner have felt when Hemant mimed a door?
qa.a: He may have felt willing to help but uncertain what Hemant wanted, which is why he offered a lock instead.

grounding: Chat about a worker in a new city using shapes, mime and pointing to make a request and checking with a photo to avoid mix-ups.

subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
passage: Kamal had just started at the brick kiln outside Ranchi, and his Hindi was thin. On his second morning he needed a wheelbarrow with a flat tyre swapped. He pointed at the wheel, made a hissing sound and spread his hands to show air going out. The foreman, Rukmini's uncle, understood and waved him toward the shed. But when Kamal drew a circle in the air to mean "wheel", the man beside him thought he meant the whole team should circle up. They laughed together. Kamal took out his phone, showed a picture of the tyre and said, "Yeh?" The uncle nodded. "Haan, yeh." The tyre was changed within minutes.

qa.a: He started at a brick kiln outside Ranchi.

qa.q: What did Kamal's picture and "Yeh?" show about his thinking?
qa.a: It showed he wanted to be sure the request was understood, since his air circle had been misread. The laughing suggests the mix-up was harmless.

qa.q: What worked to make his request clear?
qa.a: A phone picture of the tyre and the confirming word "Yeh?" made the request clear after the gestures caused confusion.

qa.q: How might the man beside Kamal have understood the circle in the air?
qa.a: He thought Kamal meant the team should circle up, so he took the gesture as a call to gather.

grounding: Third-person rural narrative of a worker in a new place using mime and pointing that can mislead, confirmed with an image.
